summary: Describes Autokey, a security model for authenticating NTP servers to clients using public key cryptography. It is designed so servers can stay stateless and timekeeping stays accurate, which IPsec or standard PKI do not suit well. It covers requirements, design principles and the protocol specification. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Autokey is a security design for NTP that lets a client check the identity of a time server. It uses certificates and public-key signatures during setup, then uses a sequence of keys derived by hashing to authenticate later packets more cheaply. RFC 5906 describes an NTPv4 implementation and notes both its protections and its limitations.

questions: how does autokey authenticate ntp servers
what is a proventic ntp source
why not use ipsec for ntp
subtitle: How NTP servers authenticate to clients while limiting per-packet cryptographic work.

tldr.problem: NTP clients need to authenticate time servers, but per-client server state and a public-key signature on every packet conflict with NTP's design and timing needs.
tldr.mechanism: Autokey uses certificates and signatures during setup, then authenticates packets with a precomputed sequence of hashed session keys carried through NTP exchanges.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5906 is an Informational description of the Autokey design and its NTPv4 implementation. It is updated by RFC 9748.

today: RFC 5906 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 9748. It has not been obsoleted and describes the Autokey design and the NTPv4 software implementation on which it was based.

sections.title: Why NTP Uses a Separate Security Design
sections.content:
NTP clients need to know that received packets came from the intended server and were not modified or replayed. The RFC argues that signing every NTP packet with public-key cryptography would harm timekeeping performance, while key-agreement systems that retain state for each client do not suit stateless servers.

Autokey combines public-key certificates and signatures with a sequence of hashed session keys. The memo describes the NTP extensions as implemented in an NTPv4 software distribution and presents them as a basis for future work. A source is called proventic when the servers on its path to primary servers have been authenticated; that does not by itself mean its time is correct.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP needs to check who sent a time packet without adding heavy work to every packet. Autokey uses public-key checks during setup and cheaper checks for later packets.

sections.title: Autokey Values and the Key List
sections.content:
An NTP message authentication code contains a 32-bit key ID and a message digest. In the reference design, the key ID space is divided at the pivot value 65536. Autokey key IDs are at or above the pivot and are discarded after use; symmetric key IDs are below it.

An autokey is an MD5 hash of the source address, destination address, key ID, and cookie, producing a 128-bit value. The sender repeatedly hashes values to form a key list. It signs the final key ID and its index, then uses the list in reverse order. A receiver hashes a received key until it reaches the signed final key ID within the allowed number of steps.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender prepares a sequence of related keys and signs information about its end. A receiver can check a later key by hashing it until it reaches that signed value.

sections.title: Exchanges and Operating Modes
sections.content:
Autokey setup uses ordered request-and-response exchanges carried in NTP extension fields. The exchanges obtain parameters, certificates, identity proof, a cookie, autokey values, a signature, and leapsecond data. The sign and leapsecond exchanges occur only after the client has synchronized to a proventic source.

The RFC describes a client/server dance, a broadcast dance, and a symmetric dance. In client/server mode, a server can regenerate a cookie from the client and server addresses and a random seed without keeping state for each client. In broadcast mode a client performs setup before validating later broadcasts. In symmetric mode peers build separate key lists from a shared cookie; if both send cookie requests at once, they use the exclusive-or of the two cookie values.
sections.plainLanguage: Client and server exchange setup information in a defined order. The details differ for client/server, broadcast, and symmetric NTP modes, but later packets use the established key sequence.

sections.title: Certificates and Identity Schemes
sections.content:
An NTP secure group is a set of hosts arranged as a certificate hierarchy rooted at trusted hosts. A trusted authority creates identity keys. Hosts obtain certificates through their servers, and clients build a certificate trail that ends at a trusted host. The configured groups must form an acyclic graph.

A certificate trail alone may not prevent a man-in-the-middle attack. The reference implementation includes private certificate, trusted certificate, IFF, GQ, and MV identity schemes. IFF, GQ, and MV use challenge-and-response exchanges; the RFC describes MV as a zero-knowledge proof. The trusted-certificate scheme alone does not provide protection against that attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A client checks a chain of certificates back to a trusted host. Some configurations also use a challenge and response to check that the server has the correct group key.

sections.title: NTP Extension Fields
sections.content:
Autokey messages are extension fields between the NTP header and the message authentication code. A field identifies its version and operation, whether it is a response or error, its length, an association ID, timestamps, and a value that may include a signature. A packet may contain several responses but only one request.

The minimum extension-field length is 8 octets. The reference implementation discards packets with fields longer than 1024 octets. Timestamps let a receiver discard old or duplicate fields before spending time verifying a signature.
sections.plainLanguage: An extension field adds an Autokey request or response to an NTP packet. Its operation and timestamps help the receiver match exchanges and reject old messages.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
The authors state that the protocol has not had a formal security analysis. They describe preliminary protections against lost, duplicate, bogus, and replayed packets. In broadcast mode, timestamps let a client reject old responses. The trusted-certificate identity scheme is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack unless another identity scheme is used.

Autokey also has clogging risks because public-key operations use resources. A server without per-client state has no obvious way to prevent rapid replay of cookie requests. Replaying old or out-of-order messages before synchronization can also prevent an exchange from completing.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes protections against several packet attacks but says the design has not received formal analysis. An attacker may still consume resources or disrupt setup by replaying messages.
